data.name: Tryphosa
data.long_meaning: In Greek, Tryphosa is derived from the Greek word tryphe, which means 'delight' or 'lovely'. It was the name of a Christian woman in ancient Rome who was known for her deep faith and commitment to Christ. She was martyred for her beliefs and is now venerated as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

in_english.name: Tryphosa
in_english.long_meaning: The name Tryphosa originates from the Hebrew word tryphosa, meaning 'to delight in pleasure' or 'to indulge in luxury'. In the New Testament, Tryphosa is mentioned as one of the women who worked hard alongside Paul, demonstrating her industrious and diligent nature. Tryphosa's name is associated with qualities such as generosity, kindness, and a strong sense of community. In Christian tradition, Tryphosa is seen as a symbol of the importance of finding joy and contentment in life, despite the challenges and hardships that may arise.

biblical_reference.note: Tryphosa is mentioned alongside Tryphaena as a member of the early Christian community in Rome, known for their hard work and diligence.

saint_reference.note: Saint Tryphosa is recognized as a martyr and a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church, celebrated on August 1st. Her feast day commemorates her bravery and selflessness in the face of persecution.

data.cultural_impact: Tryphosa was a name that stood out during the time of Roman persecution of Christians. It signified the joy and beauty found in the faith of these early believers, despite the hardships and suffering they faced. It was a reminder of the power and resilience of the Christian community and its enduring impact on Roman society.
data.spiritual_significance: For Christians named Tryphosa, the name holds a deep spiritual significance as a reminder of the joy and beauty found in a deep faith in Christ. The name reflects the commitment and love that seems 'lovely' in the eyes of God. It also carries the memory of the nameless Christian woman, Tryphosa, who embodied the strength and resilience of the faith. Her story inspires those named Tryphosa to live a life marked by deep faith and unwavering commitment to Christ.

historical_references.reference: Tryphosa, a Christian martyr in Rome during the Neronian persecution (AD 64), was a woman who converted to Christianity along with her mother, Aesia, and her sister, Tryphosa. They were arrested and sentenced to death for their faith. Tryphosa's name suggests Greek origins, possibly from the city of Triphylia in northern Greece.

Tryphosa is also mentioned in the Acts of Trypho, a late 2nd- or early 3rd-century, apocryphal text, as a Christian woman from Syria who converted her husband, Trypho, to Christianity. In this text, Tryphosa witnesses to her faith and persuades her husband to be baptized. The text is an example of early Christian literature that explores the theme of marital conversion.
